summary: Elizabeth Lopatto recounts the opening statements in Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial and argues the defense undermined itself. Prosecutor Thane Rehn said Bankman-Fried's lifestyle was "built on lies" and that he stole billions, while defense attorney Mark Cohen's plane metaphor drew attention to FTX's missing chief risk officer. The first prosecution witness, customer Marc-Antoine Julliard, described trusting FTX because of Bankman-Fried's image, ads and VC backing before his money got stuck.
one_line: Opinion account of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial openings, arguing Mark Cohen's defense highlighted FTX's missing risk officer and the prosecution's first witness was damaging.
key_facts: Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn told the jury Bankman-Fried's luxury lifestyle, including a $30 million penthouse and time with Tom Brady, was "built on lies."
Rehn said Bankman-Fried "stole billions of dollars from thousands of people" and avoided explaining cryptocurrency to the jury.

Per the prosecution, in May and June of 2022 Alameda Research lacked enough to pay its bills and pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the FTX balance sheet hole was too big to repay customers.
After CoinDesk published its article in November 2022, Bankman-Fried tweeted "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" and "We don't invest customer assets even in treasuries."
Bankman-Fried had never been offered a plea deal because he and his attorneys told the government they wouldn't negotiate.
Defense attorney Mark Cohen likened a startup to building a plane while flying it, with FTX flying into the perfect storm of the crypto crash, and conceded FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer."
Lopatto argues the missing risk officer is damaging because FTX was a futures exchange that sits between winners and losers of bets, so risk management is crucial.

Cohen argued FTX's and Alameda's business relationships were "reasonable under the circumstances" and that Bankman-Fried was too busy as CEO to oversee everything, also blaming Caroline Ellison and Changpeng "CZ" Zhao.

The first prosecution witness, Marc-Antoine Julliard, born in Paris and living in London, trusted FTX because of Bankman-Fried's image, its top-three exchange size, major VC investment and glossy ads featuring Gisele Bündchen.
Julliard was unable to withdraw on November 8th about $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin worth roughly $20,000 each, about $100,000 in total.
On cross-examination Cohen noted Julliard was a licensed commodities broker, knew crypto was risky, traded it to avoid disclosure, and didn't review the terms of service.
The next witness was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.
Bankman-Fried appeared still in court, with shorn hair from a fellow prisoner, a discounted Macy's suit, and apparent weight loss.
